seo.title: uv Python Tutorial #1 — Install uv the Right Way (and why NOT pip) (2026)
altTitles: How to install uv — and why pip install uv is the wrong route
seo.description: Chapter one of the uv course. The one line that installs uv on a machine with no Python, what curl pipe sh actually does, why PATH means you must restart your terminal, and why pip install uv is the route to avoid.
seo.breakdown: how to get uv onto your machine, and why a tool that installs Python cannot itself require Python.

scenes.narration: A tool whose job is installing Python. Written in Python. Do you see the problem?

This is the whole installation. One line, pasted into a terminal, on a machine that has no Python on it whatsoever. Fifteen seconds later uv is there and working. By the end of this chapter you'll understand every part of what that line just did.

uvStage.headline: The whole [install]
uvStage.premise: A machine with no Python at all. One line, and uv is on it.

steps.label: curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
steps.detail: no Python involved at any point

scenes.narration: Welcome back. This chapter gets uv onto your machine, and more importantly it explains why installing uv works so differently from installing anything else in the Python world.

data.title: Installing uv
data.subtitle: uv, chapter one · and the chicken-and-egg problem

scenes.narration: Start with the problem, because the problem is what makes the solution make sense.

Here's something about pip almost nobody says out loud. Pip is a Python package. Pip lives inside a Python installation, in a folder called site-packages, right alongside every other package you've ever installed. Ask pip where pip is, and pip will tell you.

uvStage.headline: pip lives [inside] Python
uvStage.premise: pip is a Python package, so pip needs a working Python before pip can run.

steps.label: python -m pip --version
steps.detail: read the path — pip is in there

scenes.narration: Which means pip can never fix a broken Python, because pip needs that Python in order to start. Break the interpreter and pip goes down with the interpreter. Now, none of that is a bug, and none of it is pip's fault. Living inside Python is simply what pip is.

uvStage.headline: Break Python, [lose pip]
uvStage.premise: Whatever lives inside the interpreter cannot outlive the interpreter.

steps.label: python -m pip install anything
steps.detail: the package-fixer is itself a package

stage.label: CPython 3.12
stage.sub: broken, missing, or the wrong version

stage.label: uv
stage.sub: one binary, standing on the floor

scenes.narration: So uv is built the other way round. uv is one compiled program, written in Rust, sitting beside Python rather than inside Python. uv needs no interpreter to start, which is exactly why a single line of curl works on a bare machine, and why in a few chapters uv can download an entire Python for you on demand.

uvStage.headline: uv sits [beside] Python
uvStage.premise: One compiled binary on the floor. Nothing underneath it to break.

steps.label: file $(which uv)
steps.detail: statically linked: it carries its own world

stage.label: uv
stage.sub: a Rust binary, on the floor
stage.detail: which is why curl alone is enough

scenes.narration: There are several roads onto your machine and they all end at the same binary. Mac and Linux use curl. Windows uses PowerShell. Homebrew works, and so does winget. And then there's the fourth road, which is the one to avoid.

uvStage.headline: Four roads, [one] binary
uvStage.premise: Every route below installs the identical program. Only the delivery differs.

steps.label: uv --version
steps.detail: the same answer from every road

scenes.narration: Why is that fourth road a trap? Because pip puts uv inside a Python environment, and managing Python environments from the outside is uv's whole job. Delete the environment and uv disappears along with the environment. Worse, uv can no longer update itself, because a package cannot overwrite its own file while Python is holding that file open.

uvStage.headline: Why pip install uv is a [trap]
uvStage.premise: Installing the manager inside the thing it manages puts it back in the trap.

steps.label: uv self update
out: error: Self-update is only available for uv
binaries installed via the standalone installer
steps.detail: the one route where updating breaks

scenes.narration: Now let's read that install line properly, because you should never paste something into a terminal you cannot read.

chapter.title: Read it before you run it
chapter.subtitle: what curl pipe sh does

scenes.narration: Curl fetches a file over the internet. Dash L follows redirects. Dash s stays quiet. Dash S still shows real errors. Dash f fails properly on a bad response instead of saving the error page. Then the pipe hands that file to sh, which runs it. That's it — download a script, run the script.

uvStage.headline: What [curl pipe sh] means
uvStage.premise: Four flags and a pipe. Nothing hidden, nothing clever.

steps.label: curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh -o install.sh
steps.detail: -o writes a file instead of piping

steps.label: head -3 install.sh
steps.detail: an ordinary shell script. read it.

steps.label: sh install.sh
steps.detail: read first, then run. always allowed.

scenes.narration: On Windows the shape is identical. PowerShell fetches the script with irm, and iex runs it. Same binary, same destination, different shell.

uvStage.headline: The same thing, on [Windows]
uvStage.premise: irm fetches, iex runs. The shell differs; the binary does not.

steps.label: powershell -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex"
steps.detail: irm fetches. iex runs. same two jobs.

scenes.narration: And now the step that trips up literally everybody, the first time.

When you type a command, your shell doesn't search your whole computer. Your shell walks a short list of folders, in order, and runs the first match found. The list is called PATH. The installer put uv in a folder near the end of the list, then added that folder to your shell profile.

uvStage.headline: PATH is a [short list]
uvStage.premise: Your shell checks these folders in order and runs the first match it finds.

steps.label: which uv
steps.detail: found, on the fourth folder checked

stage.label: ~/.local/bin
stage.sub: and uv is in this one

scenes.narration: But your open terminal read the profile once, back when the terminal started, and no shell re-reads a profile on its own. So the first thing almost everybody sees after installing uv is command not found, and almost everybody assumes the install failed. The install did not fail. Close the terminal, open a fresh one, and uv is right there.

uvStage.headline: Close it. [Open] a new one.
uvStage.premise: A shell reads its profile once, at startup. Yours started before uv existed.

steps.label: uv --version
steps.detail: installed fine. this shell has an old list.

steps.label: exec $SHELL   # or just open a new terminal
steps.detail: now the profile is read again

steps.label: uv --version
steps.detail: there it is

scenes.narration: The version line is worth reading properly, because three separate facts live in it. First the version number. Then the exact commit the binary was built from. Then the build date. When you report a bug or follow along with a tutorial, the commit hash is what tells another person precisely which uv you are running, down to the day.

uvStage.headline: Read the [version] line
uvStage.premise: Three facts in one line: the version, the exact commit, and the build date.

steps.label: uv --version
steps.detail: version, commit, date, platform

steps.label: uv self update
out: You are on the latest version of uv (0.12.5)
steps.detail: and this only works off the standalone route

steps.label: uv --help | head -3
out: An extremely fast Python package manager.
steps.detail: and that one line is the whole pitch

scenes.narration: uv keeps its own things in three folders, and it will tell you where all three are. The cache is where downloads are kept so the second install is instant. The tool folder holds programs you install. The python folder holds interpreters uv downloaded for you. These live in different places on Windows and on Unix, and uv knows which.

uvStage.headline: Three folders uv [owns]
uvStage.premise: Ask uv where its own things live. It answers, correctly, on either platform.

steps.label: uv cache dir
steps.detail: Windows: AppData\Local\uv\cache

steps.label: uv tool dir
steps.detail: Windows: AppData\Roaming\uv\tools

steps.label: uv python dir
steps.detail: Windows: AppData\Roaming\uv\python

scenes.narration: Quick check. Of those four roads, why is pip install uv the one to avoid? Pause here and have a proper think about it. Ready? Because pip puts uv inside a Python environment, and managing those from outside is uv's whole job.

quiz.question: Why avoid installing uv with pip?

options.text: It puts uv inside what uv manages

quiz.why: Delete that environment and uv goes too — and it cannot self-update.

scenes.narration: And because uv is only ever files in folders, removing uv takes three commands and no control panel at all. Clear the cache, delete the tool and python folders, delete the binary. Nothing else on your machine ever knew uv was there.

uvStage.headline: Uninstalling is [three] commands
uvStage.premise: No installer, no registry, no uninstall wizard. Three folders, gone.

steps.label: uv cache clean
steps.detail: take the downloads with it

steps.label: rm -r "$(uv tool dir)" "$(uv python dir)"
steps.detail: the tools and the interpreters

steps.label: rm ~/.local/bin/uv ~/.local/bin/uvx
steps.detail: and the binary itself. done.

scenes.narration: One last thing the installer deliberately does not do. uv does not touch your system Python, does not modify any environment you already have, and does not put a bare python command on your PATH. Everything uv installs lives in uv's own folders, which is why removing uv leaves absolutely nothing behind.

uvStage.headline: What the installer [never] touches
uvStage.premise: Two folders written, and nothing at all changed in any Python you already had.

steps.label: which python python3 uv uvx
steps.detail: your python3 is exactly where it was

stage.label: your existing venvs
stage.sub: uv has not looked at them yet

stage.label: bare `python`
stage.sub: uv will not shadow a command you rely on

stage.label: ~/.local/bin
stage.sub: uv and uvx. that is the whole footprint.

scenes.narration: So, to recap. pip lives inside Python, so pip can never rescue a Python that's broken. uv is one compiled binary that sits beside Python, which is why a single line installs it on a bare machine. And when the terminal says command not found, open a new terminal.

points.text: pip lives inside Python. uv sits beside it.
One binary, four roads, and pip is the trap
Command not found? Open a new terminal.
